## Approach

To extend the sentiment analysis example used in Chapter 2 of the *Text Mining with R* textbook, I will start by first reproducing the example code from Chapter 2. I do not anticipate any issues with this as it will be mostly copying and pasting with potential minor tweaks to fit my needs. Then I will extend the analysis in two ways, according to the lab requirements.

1.  Firstly I will use a different text corpus. The corpus I would like to use is Social Media or Tweets specifically (if possible). I thought this would be interesting as the example used in Chapter 2, was for an old book while these lexicons are validated typically with twitter data. So I assume the lagnuage would be a more natural fit. Also since I have not performed any Sentiment analysis before I would like to work with a more modern text corpus. Since I am inexperienced, I may change my text corpus if there are any issues with using Tweet data to something simpler, and I anticipate having some trouble getting everything adjusted because of my lack of experience.
2.  Lastly I will add an additional sentiment lexicon, which I will likely draw from another R package. I am currently unsure of which lexicon specifically, but I will update my conclusion with my choice when I submit my code base along with any other unforeseen results and challenges.

## Code Base

```{r load-packages}
library(janeaustenr)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(ggplot2)
library(wordcloud)
library(reshape2)
library(tidyverse)
library(gutenbergr)
library(syuzhet)

alice <- gutenberg_download(11)
```

1

```{r count-joy}
tidy_books <- austen_books() %>%
  group_by(book) %>%
  mutate(
    linenumber = row_number(),
    chapter = cumsum(str_detect(text, 
                                regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]", 
                                      ignore_case = TRUE)))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

nrc_joy <- get_sentiments("nrc") %>% 
  filter(sentiment == "joy")

tidy_books %>%
  filter(book == "Emma") %>%
  inner_join(nrc_joy) %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r plot-sentiment-scores}
jane_austen_sentiment <- tidy_books %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing")) %>%
  count(book, index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>% 
  mutate(sentiment = positive - negative)

ggplot(jane_austen_sentiment, aes(index, sentiment, fill = book)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~book, ncol = 2, scales = "free_x")
```

```{r comparing-lexicons}
pride_prejudice <- tidy_books %>% 
  filter(book == "Pride & Prejudice")

afinn <- pride_prejudice %>% 
  inner_join(get_sentiments("afinn")) %>% 
  group_by(index = linenumber %/% 80) %>% 
  summarise(sentiment = sum(value)) %>% 
  mutate(method = "AFINN")

bing_and_nrc <- bind_rows(
  pride_prejudice %>% 
    inner_join(get_sentiments("bing")) %>%
    mutate(method = "Bing et al."),
  pride_prejudice %>% 
    inner_join(get_sentiments("nrc") %>% 
                 filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", 
                                         "negative"))
    ) %>%
    mutate(method = "NRC")) %>%
  count(method, index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0) %>% 
  mutate(sentiment = positive - negative)

bind_rows(afinn, 
          bing_and_nrc) %>%
  ggplot(aes(index, sentiment, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y")

```

```{r nrc-lexicon}
get_sentiments("nrc") %>% 
  filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")) %>%

get_sentiments("bing") %>%
```

# Alice In Wonderland

```{r alice-in-wonderland}
glimpse(alice)

tidy_alice <- alice %>%
  mutate(linenumber = row_number()) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

alice_sentiment <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") %>%
  count(index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(sentiment_score = positive - negative)

ggplot(alice_sentiment,
       aes(x = index, y = sentiment_score)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Sentiment Throughout Alice's Adventures in Wonderland",
    x = "Section of Book",
    y = "Net Sentiment Score"
  )

```

```{r Jockers-sentiment}
jockers <- get_sentiment_dictionary("syuzhet") %>%
  as_tibble()

head(jockers)

alice_jockers <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(jockers, by = "word") %>%
  group_by(index = linenumber %/% 80) %>%
  summarise(
    sentiment_score = sum(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(alice_jockers,
       aes(x = index, y = sentiment_score)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Sentiment in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (Syuzhet)",
    x = "Section of Book",
    y = "Net Sentiment Score"
  )
```

```{r combined-lexicons}
alice_comparison <- bind_rows(
  alice_sentiment %>%
    select(index, sentiment_score) %>%
    mutate(method = "Bing"),

  alice_jockers %>%
    select(index, sentiment_score) %>%
    mutate(method = "Syuzhet")
)

ggplot(alice_comparison,
       aes(x = index, y = sentiment_score)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(
    ~method,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Sentiment Lexicons",
    subtitle = "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland",
    x = "Section of Book (80 lines)",
    y = "Net Sentiment Score"
  )
```

# Conclusions and Analysis:

To further extend the lab I decided to use a part of the book *Alice in Wonderland* by Lewis Carroll to analyze. This was done using the Bing and Syuzhet sentiment lexicons. While the Bing lexicons classifies words as either positive, or negative which allows the net sentiment to be calculated by subtracting the number of positive words from the number of negative ones. In contrast, the Syuzhet numerical sentiment values for individual words, which can be added together to calculate the net sentiment for sections of the novel. There were both similarities and differences between the lexicons sentiments of the book. For example both lexicons interpreted section 7 as negative but the Bing lexicon weigh it much more negative. Overall however, Syuzhet interpreted the most sections more positively than the Bing lexicons.

In conclusion, comparing sentiment lexicons shows that both can have very interpretations of the same text. While they were similarities, these lexicons scored many sections differently, and with different intensity. Factors like how these words are scored and the purpose in which they are to be used will heavily influence their interpretations of the passage. For example using modern tools to train lexicons like social media, may influence how they would interpret older literature as the meaning and connotation behind words can change over time. Also it is worth noting that scoring individual words may miss the context of the entire sentence, or thought. Things like sarcasm, and negation (words like "not" preceding a word) will not be scored accurately. So while helpful, context would need to be applied when interpreting sentiment scores.

```{r four-lexicon-graph}

# 1. Bing sentiment
alice_bing <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("bing"), by = "word") %>%
  count(index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sentiment_score = positive - negative,
    method = "Bing"
  )

# 2. AFINN sentiment
alice_afinn <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(get_sentiments("afinn"), by = "word") %>%
  group_by(index = linenumber %/% 80) %>%
  summarise(
    sentiment_score = sum(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(method = "AFINN")

# 3. NRC sentiment
alice_nrc <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(
    get_sentiments("nrc") %>%
      filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")),
    by = "word"
  ) %>%
  count(index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    sentiment_score = positive - negative,
    method = "NRC"
  )

# 4. Syuzhet sentiment
jockers <- get_sentiment_dictionary("syuzhet") %>%
  as_tibble()

alice_syuzhet <- tidy_alice %>%
  inner_join(jockers, by = "word") %>%
  group_by(index = linenumber %/% 80) %>%
  summarise(
    sentiment_score = sum(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(method = "Syuzhet")

# 5. Combine all four results
alice_all_lexicons <- bind_rows(
  alice_bing,
  alice_afinn,
  alice_nrc,
  alice_syuzhet
) %>%
  select(index, sentiment_score, method)

# 6. Create the comparison graph
ggplot(alice_all_lexicons,
       aes(x = index, y = sentiment_score, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~method,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Four Sentiment Lexicons",
    subtitle = "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland",
    x = "Section of Book (80 lines)",
    y = "Net Sentiment Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
